chapter_theme: Communicating what can't be said. Thread within crystal, scent within a bud, and the movement of her gaze from bangles to shoulders to feet: unspoken signs carry the fear of a new parting and the resolve to go with him. It is the book's mature counterpart to the first signs of chapter 110.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar sets this after a reunion, when the man's new tenderness makes her fear another departure. In his plan, the man speaks in 1271-1275, the woman in 1276-1278, her friend in 1279, and the man in 1280. Manakkudavar gives 1275 and 1280 to the friend and often reads the verses as belonging to courtship.

1271.reading: The man tells her that though she hides it, her kohl-lined eyes have gone beyond her control and have something they want to say.
1271.nuance: In Parimelazhagar's setting the man has returned and is lavishing affection on her, and she takes fright, which makes this a kind of tragic misunderstanding. Kalaignar has the eyes declare love that resists separation. The verse only says there is something.

1272.reading: The man says this artless girl who fills his eyes, with her bamboo shoulders, has a great measure of womanly nature.
1272.nuance: The compliment may be a rebuke. Parimelazhagar glosses நீர்மை as மடமை, 'naivety', and has him complain to her friend that she fears a separation he has no thought of. Kalaignar takes it as simple praise.

1273.reading: The man says that, like the thread that shows in strung gems, there is something that shows through this young woman's beauty.
1273.nuance: The gem image needs transparent stones, and Parimelazhagar says crystal: inside but visible. What is inside isn't compatible with the outer beauty, he says, but appears with it.

positions.position: It's an intent that he can't himself identify, and he asks her friend to find out what it is.
positions.quote: மடந்தையது அணியகத்துக் கிடந்து புறத்துப் புலனாகின்றதொரு குறிப்பு உண்டு.

positions.position: It's a hidden sorrow, which shows though she conceals it.

1274.reading: The man says there is something within the bud of this girl's smile, like the scent within a closed bud.
1274.nuance: It's a companion to 1273, except that here nothing shows: scent inside a bud can't be perceived, so his certainty about it is a matter of faith. Manakkudavar sets it in courtship, with the man telling his own heart that her smile promises joy, and Kalaignar says the smile holds the memory of her lover.

1275.reading: The stealth with which the tight-bangled woman slipped away holds a medicine for great sorrow; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man tells the friend that she has hidden from him out of a false fear, and the cure is for the friend to explain that he isn't leaving.
positions.quote: என்கண் இல்லாத தொன்றனை உட்கொண்டு அது காரணமாக என்னை மறைத்துப் போன குறிப்பு

positions.position: The friend tells the man, in courtship, that the woman's slipping away coyly means that his plea will succeed.
positions.quote: எதிர்ப்பட்ட தலைமகற்கு நின்குறை முடியும்; நீ இவ்விடைச் செல்லென்று தோழி கூறியது.

1276.reading: The woman tells her friend that his great comfort and eager lovemaking contains in it her having to endure hardship again and to think about his lack of love.
1276.nuance: A sad piece of reading. His tenderness is the very thing that gives him away, since she reasons from excess of kindness to a coming parting. Both older commentators give it to her, speaking to the friend.

1277.reading: The woman says her bangles knew before she did that the lord of the cool shore had parted from her.
1277.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes the separation inward: he is still physically with her but has left in his mind. Her body has registered this before her understanding did. So bangles, the book's most public symptom, are here her private source of knowledge.

1278.reading: The woman says that her lover left only yesterday, and her body has been pale for seven days.
1278.nuance: The sum doesn't add up, on purpose. The pain started before the event, because she read it coming.

positions.position: He hasn't physically left: 'left yesterday' means he made up his mind then, shown by yesterday's tenderness.
positions.quote: 'நெருநற்றுச் செய்த தலையளியாற் பிரிவு துணியப்பட்டது' என்பாள், 'நெருநற்றுச் சென்றார்' என்றும்

positions.position: He has actually left, and she was grieving before he went.
positions.quote: இஃது அவர் பிரிவதன் முன்னும் பிரிவரென் றேங்கி, இன்புற்றில் மென்று தலைமகள் கூறியது.

1279.reading: Parimelazhagar's speaker, the friend, tells the man that she looked at her bangles, looked at her soft shoulders and looked at her feet: this is what she did there.
1279.nuance: The whole verse is a silent gesture, and the commentators read it as a sentence: 'these will slip if you leave me; these will thin; so I'll go with you on these'. The verse itself doesn't state the conclusion. This is perhaps the most purely dramatic thing in the Kural, and the friend's 'that's what she did' leaves him to work it out.

1280.reading: Those who know say that telling love's sickness with the eyes and begging adds more womanhood to womanhood; the speaker is the man for Parimelazhagar and the friend for Manakkudavar.

positions.position: The man answers: he praises her decision to go with him, as a way of telling her friend he won't be leaving at all.
positions.quote: தன் பிரிவின்மைக் குறிப்பினை அறிவுறுப்பான், அவள் பெண்மையினைப் பிறர்மேலிட்டு வியந்து கூறியவாறு.

positions.position: The friend speaks to the man, having seen the woman's response to news of his leaving.
positions.quote: இது பிரிவுணர்த்திய தலைமகள் குறிப்புக்கண்டு தலைமகற்குத் தோழி சொல்லியது.

links.note: In Parimelazhagar's reading, 1120 is the man refusing to elope because her feet can't bear even swan's down. In 1279 she looks at those same feet, her way of saying she will walk. The compliment had been an excuse, and her glance answers it.

706 says the face shows what is in the heart, as crystal shows what is next to it, in the chapter on reading signs in court. 1273 uses crystal the same way, with a thread inside it. Courtier and lover both depend on the transparency of the surface.
In 1152 the fear of parting spoils union, and Parimelazhagar cites a poem where unusual fussing is the warning sign. 1276 makes that the very argument: too much tenderness is proof of a departure.
Both have bangles announcing the departure of the lord of the shore. In 1157 they announce it to others, and in 1277 they tell her, before she herself knows. The sign has moved inward.

source_issues: 1271: Manakkudavar's entry, flagged [#], is close to word for word Parimelazhagar's gloss.
1271, 1275-1277, 1279, 1280: Parimelazhagar's text has a character corruption in தௌ¢ where தெளி is intended.
1275: Pope's prose reads கள்ளம் as 'well-meant departure', with no support from the commentators.
